objectives: Check that an IDS is running, capturing and detecting
Trigger and recognise alerts from several different CybICS IDS rules
Explain the trade-off between missed attacks and false alarms when tuning a threshold
takeaways: An IDS only helps if it is running, capturing the right network and producing alerts.
Traffic that passes while capture is stopped leaves no trace, so start the IDS before you test it.
Several different rules firing proves the pipeline better than one rule firing many times.
Lower thresholds catch more attacks but raise false alarms; exemptions cut noise but create blind spots.
Monitoring needs routine: test it, watch its health and make sure someone reads the alerts.

checkpoints.question: You lower the Modbus write threshold from 10 to 2 writes in 30 seconds. What is the most likely effect?
options: Fewer alerts, as fewer writes are counted
Slow attacks caught, more false alarms
Only modbus_flood alerts become faster
No change, the exemptions still apply
checkpoints.explanation: A lower threshold is more sensitive. It catches low-and-slow writes but also flags legitimate clients that are not exempt and write occasionally, which is the classic false-positive cost. Exemptions only cover hwio and FUXA, so other writers are affected.

quiz.question: You ran a port scan, then started the IDS. Why does the dashboard show no port_scan alert?
options: Alerts appear only after a 30 s delay
The IDS sees only traffic while capturing
The scan was too slow for the threshold
Port scans need the dashboard to be open
quiz.explanation: The IDS reads live packets; it has no recording of what happened before capture started. Start it first, then test. The 30-second cooldown limits repeat alerts but does not delay the first one.

quiz.question: You send 200 Modbus writes from the attack machine. How many different rules can this one activity count towards in the check?
options: Exactly one rule, modbus_flood
Up to two, depending on the rate
Up to three, with modbus_diagnostic
None, Modbus writes are trusted
quiz.explanation: Writes feed both modbus_unauth_write and modbus_flood, and a fast burst can trigger both. modbus_diagnostic only matches function codes 8 and 43, not writes, and only hwio and FUXA are trusted. You still need one more kind of activity, such as a scan, for three different rules.

quiz.question: Which situations leave a plant without detection even though the IDS container exists? (Select all that apply)
options: Capture was stopped and never restarted
The IDS listens on the wrong interface
Several rules fired in the last hour
Alerts appear but nobody reviews them
quiz.explanation: Each breaks a link in the chain from packet to response. Recent alerts from several rules may look alarming, but they are the sign of a healthy pipeline, which is exactly what the check asks for.

quiz.question: CybICS trusts Modbus writes from hwio and FUXA. What is the risk of that exemption?
options: None, writes from them are always normal
A hijacked hwio or FUXA writes unseen
Their writes still count toward modbus_flood
The HMI no longer shows any IDS alerts
quiz.explanation: Exemptions remove noise from normal traffic but blind the write rules to that host, so a compromised hwio or FUXA can write without an alert. Both are exempt from modbus_flood as well. Other controls, such as process checks, must cover the trusted hosts.

quiz.question: What is a good routine for knowing that detection still works next month?
options: Raise thresholds so only real attacks alert
Test regularly and alert on capture loss
Clear the alert buffer at the end of each day
Trust a quiet dashboard as a healthy sign
quiz.explanation: A known test proves the pipeline end to end, and a health alert catches a silent outage. A quiet dashboard is not proof of safety; it can just mean the IDS is blind, and higher thresholds only make it blinder.
